newsitem.title: RUSSIA: U.S. surgeon sees Yeltsin surgery next week.
newsitem.headline: U.S. surgeon sees Yeltsin surgery next week.

text.p: Doctors, in the final stages of preparing Boris Yeltsin for his heart operation, could operate on the Russian leader as early as next week.

Top U.S. surgeon Michael DeBakey said he was getting ready to fly to Moscow and would meet the president's doctors on Monday to decide if Yeltsin was ready for surgery and fix a final date for the planned operation.
DeBakey, the 88-year-old pioneer of bypass surgery, said on BBC radio that the operation carried of a risk of "maybe two, three, four percent".
The 65-year-old Kremlin leader "should be able to have another 10 years of good work life" assuming the operation to improve the flow of blood to the heart was successful, he added.
DeBakey, in separate comments to Reuters, said doctors were aiming to operate next week, although a firm date had not been fixed.
"We're shooting for next week," said DeBakey, who is acting as a consultant for the operation.
He said a minimum of three and probably four bypasses would be required, but the risk from the operation was low.

Debakey, speaking in his home base in Houston, Texas, said he was making flight reservations and changing his schedule in preparation for his trip to Russia. Kremlin officials said they expected DeBakey to arrive in Moscow on Monday.
Asked if Yeltsin was considered strong enough for surgery, DeBakey said: "I hope so. I can't say definitely until I get there. That's one of the reasons I'm going to check on all that."
Late on Tuesday the Kremlin issued the first of what it said would be a regular series of health bulletins on the president, who is resting at a sanatorium outside Moscow.
"The main aim of the final stage of the preparation is to bring the patient to the peak of his current physical and physiological capabilities," the bulletin said.
It said all Yeltsin's meetings had been cancelled to allow for final preparations for the operation.
Yeltsin had two heart attacks last year and is believed to have had a third before his reelection in July for a new four-year term at the helm of the world's largest country.

He said on September 5 that doctors had recommended bypass surgery and has moved to restore stability in the organs of state after weeks of public squabbling among officials trying to increase their influence during his illness.

On Tuesday he appointed two new officials to his policy-making Security Council to back up new secretary Ivan Rybkin. Rybkin's predecessor, Alexander Lebed, was sacked earlier this month for his overt presidential ambitions.
Yeltsin also threatened to crack the whip over Russia's 89 regions, many of which are fractious and independence-minded.
Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, seen as a reliable pair of hands, has been given extra powers and will formally take the helm during Yeltsin's operation.

DeBakey, in his comments to the British Broadcasting Corporation, said he was planning to meet Yeltsin's doctors on Monday. "We'll probably be meeting on Monday with the medical team and making that decision -- exact date," he said.
DeBakey said most medical problems holding up the surgery had been corrected. "So we're about ready to go."
Asked to detail the problems, he said: "The anaemia and the blood loss, and efforts to determine its source, the thyroid disfunction and the cardiac improvement."

The surgery is to be performed by Russian cardiologist Renat Akchurin, who trained under DeBakey. Akchurin visited Houston recently to familiarise himself with equipment that DeBakey said has now been sent to Moscow.
